item.title: Special Issue Proposals
item.content:encoded:
The Editors of the Human Resource Management Journal (HRMJ) invite applications for special issue proposals on themes related to the core aims and scope of the Journal. Special issue proposals will need to be cutting edge in terms of theoretical contributions, methodological innovation and rigour, with a level of critical scholarship that engages with policy and/or practice.

Timeline

  • August 25, 2026: Submission deadline for special issue proposals
item.author: Human Resource Management Journal (WILEY)

item.title: From Human Resource Management (HRM) to Artificial Intelligence Management (AIM)? — Algorithms and the Changing Governance of People at Work
item.content:encoded:
This special issue explores the fundamental shift from traditional Human Resource Management (HRM) to Artificial Intelligence Management (AIM), examining how algorithms are reshaping the governance of people at work. As organizations increasingly deploy algorithmic systems to manage recruitment, performance evaluation, scheduling, and other HR functions, we need to critically understand the implications for workers, organizations, and society.

The collection seeks to bring together diverse perspectives on how algorithms are transforming workplace governance, the mechanisms through which algorithmic management operates, and the consequences for employment relationships, worker agency, and organizational practices. We welcome contributions that examine both the promises and perils of algorithmic management across different sectors, geographies, and worker populations.

Potential topics

  • AI and algorithmic management in organizational contexts
  • The role of algorithms in HR decision-making and workforce management
  • Transformation of HR practices through artificial intelligence
  • Governance of people at work in the age of algorithms
  • Impact of AI on employment relationships and worker autonomy
  • Ethical considerations in algorithmic management
  • Data-driven HR and talent management systems
  • Worker surveillance and monitoring through algorithms
  • Resistance and adaptation to algorithmic management
  • Regulatory and policy frameworks for AI in HR

Timeline

  • October 15, 2026: Extended abstract submission deadline

item.title: New Vistas for Human Resources Management Research in the Global South
item.content:encoded:
Edwina Pio, Auckland University of Technology

Stephen Kalilpakdee, Assumption University of Thailand

This special issue seeks to advance Human Resources Management (HRM) research by centering perspectives, experiences, and contexts from the Global South. While HRM scholarship has traditionally been dominated by Western theoretical frameworks and assumptions, there is a critical need to develop contextually-grounded HRM knowledge that reflects the unique institutional, economic, social, and cultural realities of countries and regions in Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Middle East, and other parts of the Global South.

The special issue welcomes empirical studies, theoretical contributions, critical reviews, and methodological innovations that challenge dominant HRM paradigms and offer new insights into how organizations manage human resources in Global South contexts. We are particularly interested in research that moves beyond adapting Western HRM models and instead develops indigenous, culturally-sensitive, and locally-relevant approaches to understanding people management.

Contributors are encouraged to engage with diverse epistemologies, research methodologies, and analytical frameworks that honor the complexity and diversity of HRM practices across the Global South. This includes qualitative, quantitative, mixed-methods, and participatory action research approaches that center local voices and experiences.

Potential topics

  • Exploring alternative theoretical frameworks and paradigms for HRM in the Global South
  • Indigenous and culturally-rooted HRM approaches and practices
  • HRM in informal economies and non-traditional work arrangements
  • Human agency, worker voice, and resistance in HRM systems
  • HRM's role in addressing inequality, social justice, and sustainable development
  • Technology, digitalization, and their impacts on HRM in emerging economies
  • HRM in post-colonial and transitional contexts
  • Labor standards, worker protection, and ethical HRM practices in the Global South
  • Comparative HRM studies across Global South regions
  • Organizational learning and knowledge management in Global South contexts

Timeline

  • December 1, 2026: Submission window

item.title: Overqualification and Sustainable Talent Management: Challenges and Opportunities for Human Resource Management
item.content:encoded:
Asta Luksyte, +affiliation not provided in source

Overqualification—when employees possess education, skills, or experience exceeding job requirements—represents a significant and growing challenge in contemporary organizations. This phenomenon has become increasingly prevalent due to economic fluctuations, technological disruption, and shifting labor market dynamics. Despite its prevalence, overqualification remains under-researched in human resource management (HRM) literature, with limited guidance for practitioners navigating its complexities.

The sustainability of talent management practices depends on effectively addressing overqualification to ensure organizational viability, employee well-being, and long-term competitive advantage. Overqualified employees often experience underutilization of their capabilities, which can lead to reduced engagement, increased turnover, and diminished organizational performance. Conversely, organizations that strategically manage overqualified talent may unlock opportunities for innovation, enhanced performance, and sustainable competitive advantage.

This special issue seeks to advance scholarly understanding of overqualification and its implications for sustainable HRM. We welcome empirical studies, theoretical contributions, and practical insights that illuminate how organizations can effectively manage overqualified talent while promoting employee well-being, organizational effectiveness, and sustainable talent management practices. Research exploring the intersection of overqualification with diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives, as well as global perspectives on this phenomenon, is particularly encouraged.

Potential topics

  • Overqualification and person-job (PJ) fit
  • Overqualification and person-organization (PO) fit
  • Overqualification and sustainable HRM practices
  • Career development and advancement opportunities for overqualified employees
  • Retention strategies for overqualified talent
  • Underemployment and its organizational consequences
  • Skills utilization and employee engagement among overqualified workers
  • Diversity, equity, and inclusion implications of overqualification
  • Global perspectives on overqualification and talent management
  • Technological change and overqualification trends
  • Organizational culture and overqualification
  • Psychological contract violations and overqualified employees
  • Training and development for overqualified talent
  • Selection and recruitment practices addressing overqualification
  • Organizational performance implications of overqualification

Timeline

  • March 1, 2027: Submission window
